U.S. Department of Justice 

Off ice of the Solicitor General 

Washington, D.C. 20530 

November 23, 2021 

Honorable Scott S. Harris 
Clerk 
Supreme Court of the United States 
Washington, D.C. 20543 

Re:    Becerra v. Empire Health Foundation, for Valley Hospital Medical Center, 

No. 20-1312 

Dear Mr. Harris: 

In our reply brief in this case (filed November 17, 2021), in which oral argument is sched-
uled  for  November  29,  2021,  we  reported  that  the  Department  of  Health  and  Human  Services 
(HHS) had “informed this Office  * * * that it ha[d] calculated the Medicare fractions for Fiscal 
Year  2019  of  hospitals  in  the  Ninth  Circuit  applying  that  court’s  interpretation”  of  42  U.S.C. 
1359ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I) (the Medicare fraction), and “that, of those hospitals, approximately 97% 
have higher Medicare fractions for that year under the Ninth Circuit’s interpretation than under the 
2004 rule (the remainder are unchanged), with a median increase of approximately 2.9% and an 
average increase of approximately 4.3%.”  Reply Br. 19-20.  HHS informed this Office that the 
calculations of those Medicare fractions for hospitals in the Ninth Circuit for Fiscal Year 2019 on 
which those statistics were based were posted on its website (Centers for Medicare & Medicaid 
Servs., HHS, Disproportionate Share Hospital (DSH), https://www.cms.gov/Medicare/Medicare-
Fee-for-Service-Payment/AcuteInpatientPPS/dsh) on November 17, 2021.   

HHS has subsequently informed this Office that the calculations of the Medicare fractions 
that were posted on its website on November 17, and which formed the basis of the statistics re-
ported in our reply brief, were inaccurate as the result of an inadvertent computational error.  HHS 
has informed this Office that those hospitals’ corrected Medicare fractions have been posted on its 
website.  HHS has further informed this Office that the correct statistics for hospitals that are eli-
gible  to  be  paid  under  the  inpatient  prospective  payment  system,  and  so  may  be  eligible  for  
disproportionate-share-hospital adjustments, in the Ninth Circuit for Fiscal Year 2019 based on 
those  corrected  Medicare  fractions  are  as  follows:    approximately  81%  of  such  hospitals  have 
higher Medicare fractions for that year under the Ninth Circuit’s interpretation than under the 2004 
rule; approximately 15% have lower Medicare fractions than under the 2004 rule; and for the re-
maining approximately 4%, the Medicare fractions were unchanged.  The average change in the 
Fiscal Year 2019 Medicare fractions for all such hospitals in the Ninth Circuit is an increase of 
1.5%, and the median change is an increase of 1.4%.

We regret the inaccurate statement in our reply brief.  I would appreciate it if you would 

circulate this letter to the Members of the Court. 

Sincerely, 

Elizabeth B. Prelogar 
Solicitor General
